doc.title: Holly Hofmann interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Classical study with Maurice Sharp and why jazz stayed her focus
summary: Studying with Maurice Sharp, who disdained jazz, and at Cleveland Institute of Music, she felt more natural in jazz than classical; they compare orchestral and jazz mistakes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I think pretty much jazz remained the thing. I was not encouraged to play jazz through really all my classical education, because I was studying with the principal flautist of the Cleveland Orchestra, Maurice Sharp, and he felt that jazz was a lesser music. And so really he was pretty rigid about it. And then when I went to, I did my undergraduate school at Cleveland Institute of Music and stayed with him for the four years, because I had an opportunity at that time to sub for him at the Cleveland Orchestra. And that really made me want to go there to school. And at that time it was really frowned on in terms of getting a conservatory education. You were not to be out playing gigs and doing anything other than the classical, and frankly I didn’t have much time to pursue it during those years because school took all my attention.
Is there anything in jazz that you’ve done as nerve wracking as playing in a symphony orchestra? That’s a personal opinion.

Well no, because I never had the chops as a classical flautist that I feel that I’m starting to get as a jazz musician. Chops make you — the command of the instrument and the idiom make you comfortable. And classical music seems like an endless study of styles and articulations and the proper ornamentation and all the things that you need to pursue for the rest of your life. Just like in jazz, I will need to pursue tunes and changes and styles there for the rest of my life. But I was never as natural at it as I am at jazz, at the classical.
And I think in jazz you have the ability to — if there’s a mistake, you can make it work in your favor, or at least you can deal with it.
If you make a mistake in an orchestra—
Ooh. Or you don’t come in at the right time.
Yes, I’ve done that. Not in performance fortunately.
